# Technical Brief: Database Storage and Transaction Internals

## 1. Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)

**WAL protocol invariant.** The core rule is: a log record describing a change must be flushed to stable storage before the corresponding dirty data page is allowed to reach disk (the "log before data" rule), and no transaction's commit is acknowledged until its commit log record is durably forced. This is the WAL rule as formalized in ARIES.

**Log sequence numbers (LSNs).** Every log record gets a monotonically increasing LSN. Data pages store a `pageLSN` recording the LSN of the last log record that modified them, which lets recovery determine whether a given update is already reflected on disk.

**ARIES as the canonical recovery algorithm.** ARIES (Algorithm for Recovery and Isolation Exploiting Semantics) defines three recovery phases (analysis, redo, undo — detailed under Crash Recovery below) and introduces the dirty page table and the distinction between physiological log records (physical effect, logical addressing within a page) and pure physical/logical records.

**Checkpointing.** Fuzzy checkpoints record just enough metadata (active transaction table, dirty page table) to bound recovery work without stalling the system, as opposed to sharp (consistent) checkpoints that quiesce all activity and flush every dirty page — fuzzy checkpoints are standard in production engines (PostgreSQL, InnoDB, SQL Server) because they don't block transaction throughput.

**Steal/no-steal and force/no-force policies.** "Steal" means an uncommitted transaction's dirty pages may be written to disk before commit (requiring undo logging); "no-steal" forbids this. "Force" means all dirty pages must be flushed at commit time (simplifying recovery but hurting performance); "no-force" allows deferred flushing (requiring redo logging). Real systems use steal/no-force, which is why both redo and undo information must be logged (hence "redo-undo" logging).

**Group commit and log buffer flushing.** Multiple concurrent transactions' commit log records are batched into a single fsync/flush of the log buffer, amortizing the fixed cost of a durable write across many transactions — a critical throughput technique in InnoDB, PostgreSQL's WAL writer, and most commercial engines.

## 2. MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control)

**Snapshot isolation via read views.** Each transaction obtains a consistent snapshot (a read view) at start (or at each statement, depending on isolation level) that determines which versions of each row are visible, based on which transactions had committed as of snapshot acquisition.

**Version chains and visibility metadata.** PostgreSQL stores versions directly in the heap with `xmin`/`xmax` system columns marking the creating/deleting transaction IDs; visibility is computed by checking these against the active snapshot and commit status in the CLOG. InnoDB instead keeps the current row version in place and chains older versions through undo logs/rollback segments referenced by a hidden `DB_ROLL_PTR`, reconstructing old versions on demand.

**Garbage collection of dead versions.** PostgreSQL's VACUUM process reclaims heap tuples whose xmax predates all active snapshots (dead tuples) and must also handle XID wraparound via freezing. InnoDB's purge thread removes undo log entries once no active transaction/view can need them.

**First-updater-wins / first-committer-wins conflict rules.** Under snapshot isolation, when two transactions try to update the same row concurrently, the engine must abort one (typically the second to attempt the write) to avoid lost updates — this is the first-updater-wins rule.

**Write skew and Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI).** Plain snapshot isolation permits write skew anomalies. PostgreSQL's SSI implementation detects dangerous structures (rw-antidependency cycles among concurrent transactions) using SIREAD locks (predicate-style read locks that don't block, only mark potential conflicts) and aborts a transaction when a cycle is detected, achieving full serializability without blocking reads.

## 3. LSM Trees (Log-Structured Merge Trees)

**Memtable and WAL pairing.** Writes go first to an in-memory sorted structure (commonly a skip list, as in LevelDB/RocksDB) and are simultaneously appended to a write-ahead log for durability; once the memtable fills, it becomes immutable and is flushed to disk as a new SSTable (Sorted String Table).

**SSTables and sparse indexing.** Each SSTable is an immutable sorted file with a block index (and often a sparse index plus block-level restart points) enabling binary search without reading the whole file; deletes are represented as tombstones rather than immediate physical removal.

**Bloom filters.** Per-SSTable bloom filters let point lookups skip SSTables that provably do not contain a key, bounding the read amplification inherent to having many SSTable levels.

**Compaction strategies.** Leveled compaction (LevelDB-style) keeps each level roughly 10x larger than the previous and merges overlapping key ranges to bound per-level duplicate data; size-tiered compaction (Cassandra-style) merges similarly-sized SSTables regardless of key range, trading more space/read amplification for lower write amplification. RocksDB's default is a leveled-tiered hybrid that tiers at L0 and levels below.

**Write/read amplification trade-off.** LSM trees convert random writes into sequential writes, reducing write cost at ingest time, but at the expense of read amplification (checking multiple levels) and periodic write amplification during compaction — a fundamental trade-off against B+trees' direct in-place update model.

## 4. B+Tree Maintenance

**Node splits and merges.** On overflow, a leaf or internal node splits into two, pushing a separator key up to the parent; on underflow after deletion, nodes may merge with a sibling or redistribute keys, maintaining the minimum occupancy invariant (typically ~50% fill factor minimum).

**Latch coupling (crabbing).** Concurrent traversal acquires a latch on a child node before releasing the latch on its parent, then releases the parent latch — "crabbing" down the tree — to allow safe concurrent reads/writes without holding the whole path locked.

**B-link trees.** To avoid holding multiple latches during splits (which hurts concurrency), B-link trees add right-sibling pointers at every level, letting a reader who arrives mid-split simply follow the right-link to find a key that moved, allowing splits to be made visible incrementally without blocking concurrent traversals.

**Prefix/suffix truncation.** Separator keys in internal nodes can be truncated to the shortest prefix that still distinguishes the left and right subtrees, reducing internal node size and increasing fan-out.

**Bulk loading and clustered vs. non-clustered maintenance cost.** Bulk loading builds a B+tree bottom-up from sorted input, avoiding the cost of incremental splits. Clustered indexes (where the leaf level is the actual row storage, as in InnoDB's primary key index) incur higher maintenance cost on updates that change the key, since row data must physically move; non-clustered (secondary) indexes only store pointers/row IDs and are cheaper to maintain but require an extra lookup.

## 5. Two-Phase Commit (2PC)

**Prepare (vote) phase and commit phase.** The coordinator sends a PREPARE message to all participants; each participant force-writes a prepare log record (durably recording its vote) before replying YES or NO. If all vote YES, the coordinator force-writes a commit record and sends COMMIT; any NO triggers ABORT to all.

**The blocking problem.** If the coordinator crashes after participants have voted YES but before they receive the final decision, participants are left "in doubt" — holding locks, unable to unilaterally commit or abort — since another participant might have received a different final message. This is 2PC's fundamental blocking property under coordinator failure.

**Three-phase commit (3PC).** 3PC adds a "pre-commit" phase between voting and the final decision specifically to eliminate this blocking window, allowing participants to use a timeout-driven protocol to safely proceed without waiting indefinitely on the coordinator, at the cost of an extra message round and still being vulnerable to certain network-partition scenarios.

**Presumed-abort and presumed-commit optimizations.** Presumed-abort lets participants assume ABORT if no record of the transaction's outcome exists, avoiding the need to write/force an abort log record on every participant. Presumed-commit does the mirror-image optimization for workloads dominated by commits, trading off differently on logging cost.

**In-doubt transaction recovery.** Participants that crash and recover must consult their local prepare/commit log records and may need to query the coordinator (or other participants) to resolve any transaction still in the "in-doubt" state.

**Relationship to consensus-based commit.** Spanner layers 2PC on top of Paxos groups: each shard's leader/replica group commits locally via Paxos, and a cross-shard transaction still runs 2PC among the involved Paxos groups, combining 2PC's atomic cross-partition commit property with Paxos's fault-tolerant replication (removing the single-coordinator-failure blocking problem at the group level, though the 2PC coordinator itself can still be a bottleneck).

## 6. Logical Clocks

**Lamport clocks and happens-before.** Lamport timestamps assign each event a scalar counter incremented on local events and updated to `max(local, received) + 1` on message receipt, giving a partial order consistent with Lamport's happens-before relation, though it cannot distinguish concurrent events from causally related ones by timestamp alone.

**Vector clocks.** Each process maintains a vector of counters, one per process, incremented locally and merged (component-wise max) on message receipt; comparing two vector clocks fully determines whether one event happened-before another, happened-after, or is concurrent with it — strictly more informative than scalar Lamport clocks.

**Version vectors.** A close relative of vector clocks used by systems like Dynamo-style stores (and the original Dynamo paper's successor systems such as Riak) to detect concurrent, conflicting writes to the same key across replicas, enabling clients or the system to recognize siblings requiring application-level conflict resolution.

**Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC).** HLC combines a physical wall-clock component with a logical counter, guaranteeing timestamps stay close to physical time while still preserving the Lamport happens-before ordering guarantee; used in CockroachDB and MongoDB to get causality tracking with human-interpretable, roughly-synchronized timestamps.

**TrueTime and bounded uncertainty.** Spanner's TrueTime API exposes an uncertainty interval `[earliest, latest]` for the current time rather than a single value, and Spanner's commit protocol waits out this uncertainty (the "commit-wait" rule) before releasing locks, which provides external consistency (equivalent to linearizability) for distributed transactions despite relying on physical clocks.

## 7. Quorum Systems

**R + W > N and quorum intersection.** For N replicas, read quorum size R and write quorum size W, choosing R + W > N guarantees that any read quorum and any write quorum intersect in at least one replica, ensuring reads can observe the latest committed write.

**Strict quorums vs. sloppy quorums.** A strict quorum requires R or W acknowledgments from the designated N replicas specifically; Dynamo's sloppy quorum instead allows writes/reads to be satisfied by any R/W of the "first N healthy nodes" encountered while walking the preference list, trading strict consistency for availability during node failures or partitions.

**Hinted handoff and read repair.** Hinted handoff temporarily routes a write meant for an unavailable node to another node, which hands it off once the original node recovers; read repair compares versions returned by a read quorum and pushes the most recent version back to stale replicas, both acting as quorum-consistency maintenance mechanisms that let sloppy quorums eventually converge.

**Majority quorums in consensus (Paxos/Raft).** Paxos and Raft require a majority (⌊N/2⌋+1) of nodes to accept a proposal/log entry, which guarantees any two majorities overlap by at least one node — this overlap is what prevents two conflicting values from both being chosen (safety), distinct from the Dynamo-style R+W>N tunable quorum used for eventual-consistency stores.

**Witness replicas and flexible quorums.** Witness (non-voting-data, voting-only) replicas participate in quorum voting for availability/fault tolerance without storing full data, reducing storage cost while preserving quorum guarantees. Flexible quorums decouple the quorum size used for leader election from the quorum size used for log commitment (e.g., using smaller "commit quorums" and larger "election quorums" or vice versa) to tune availability versus performance independently, and Paxos Quorum Leases further optimize by granting a quorum (or one node) the right to serve local reads without consulting other replicas for a lease period.

## 8. Crash Recovery

**ARIES three-phase recovery: analysis, redo, undo.** The analysis pass scans the log from the last checkpoint to reconstruct the dirty page table and the list of transactions active at crash time (the active transaction table). The redo pass replays history starting from the minimum `recLSN` in the dirty page table, reapplying every logged update whose effect might not be on disk ("repeating history," redoing even updates from transactions that will ultimately be undone). The undo pass then rolls back all transactions that were active (uncommitted) at crash time, in reverse log order.

**Repeating history.** ARIES's redo phase does not try to distinguish committed from uncommitted updates — it redoes everything since the relevant point, which simplifies the algorithm and correctly reconstructs the exact pre-crash state before undo cleans up incomplete transactions.

**Compensation Log Records (CLRs).** When undoing an update, ARIES writes a CLR describing the compensating action; CLRs are never themselves undone (they have a `nextUndoLSN` pointer instead), which guarantees the undo phase is idempotent and recovery terminates even if the system crashes again during undo.

**Dirty page table and checkpoint-bounded recovery.** The dirty page table (tracking which pages have in-memory changes not yet on disk, and the earliest LSN that dirtied them) combined with periodic fuzzy checkpoints bounds how far back the redo pass must scan, keeping recovery time proportional to activity since the last checkpoint rather than since the dawn of the database.

**Torn-write protection.** Because a crash during a partial page write can corrupt a page (a "torn page," especially problematic since database pages are often larger than the disk's atomic write unit), engines use mechanisms like InnoDB's doublewrite buffer (writing pages to a contiguous staging area before writing to their final location, so a torn page can be detected and repaired from the doublewrite copy) or full-page-image logging (PostgreSQL's full_page_writes) to guarantee recoverable pages.

**Checksums and page validation.** Page-level checksums (stored in the page header) let recovery and normal I/O detect corruption from torn writes, media errors, or bugs, triggering recovery from a redundant copy or log replay rather than silently reading corrupted data.

# Storage Engine Internals: WAL, LSM Trees, B+Tree Maintenance, and Crash Recovery

## 1. Write-Ahead Logging

### 1.1 The WAL Protocol Invariant

The foundational rule of write-ahead logging is: **a log record describing an update must reach stable storage before the corresponding modified data page is allowed to reach stable storage.** More precisely, in ARIES terms, the log record's LSN must be persisted before the data page carrying that LSN (stamped in the page header, called the `pageLSN`) is flushed to disk. This guarantees that any update visible on disk is reconstructible from the log, which is the basis for both redo (ensuring committed work survives) and undo (ensuring uncommitted work can be rolled back even after a crash mid-write).

A stricter corollary governs commit: **the commit log record for a transaction must be forced to stable storage before the transaction is reported as committed to the client** (the "log force at commit" rule, sometimes called the commit-durability rule). This is what gives WAL-based systems durability (the D in ACID) without requiring every data page touched by the transaction to be flushed synchronously.

### 1.2 Log Sequence Numbers (LSNs)

Every log record is assigned a monotonically increasing **Log Sequence Number**, typically the byte offset of the record within the log (or a logical counter mapped to an offset). LSNs serve several purposes:

- They establish total order of updates for redo replay.
- Each data page stores the LSN of the most recent log record that modified it (`pageLSN`), allowing recovery to determine, per page, which log records are already reflected in the page and which still need to be redone.
- The log manager tracks the **LSN of the next record to be written**, the **flushed LSN** (durable-up-to point), and per-transaction **last-LSN** (to support backward chaining of a transaction's log records for undo).

### 1.3 Checkpointing: Fuzzy vs. Sharp

Checkpoints bound the amount of log that must be scanned during recovery.

- **Sharp (consistent) checkpoints** quiesce the system, flush all dirty buffer pages to disk, and write a checkpoint record, guaranteeing that at checkpoint time disk and log are consistent. They are simple but stall transaction processing and are impractical for high-throughput systems.
- **Fuzzy checkpoints** (used by ARIES and virtually all production systems) do not flush all dirty pages synchronously. Instead, the checkpoint record captures the **Dirty Page Table (DPT)** — the set of currently dirty pages and their `recLSN` (the LSN of the earliest log record that made the page dirty since its last flush) — and the **Transaction Table** (active transactions and their status/last-LSN). Dirty pages are flushed asynchronously afterward. Recovery uses the minimum `recLSN` across the DPT to determine the log start point for the redo pass, so correctness is preserved without stalling.

### 1.4 Log Record Types: Physical, Physiological, Logical

- **Physical redo/undo records** capture the full before/after byte image of a changed region. Simple to apply but large and insensitive to concurrent structural changes.
- **Physiological records** (the ARIES default) describe changes at the level of a page but allow the physical representation within the page to differ between the time of logging and the time of redo — e.g., "insert record R into slot S of page P" without fixing exact byte offsets, accommodating slotted-page reorganization. This balances efficiency with page-level flexibility.
- **Logical undo records** describe the operation to be undone in terms of the operation's semantics rather than physical byte changes — essential for operations like B+tree splits, where physically undoing a structural change bears no resemblance to physically redoing it. Logical undo is paired with physical/physiological redo in ARIES: redo is always physical/physiological (idempotent, byte-level, "repeat history"), while undo can be logical, generating **compensation log records** to record the logical inverse action.

### 1.5 Group Commit

**Group commit** amortizes the cost of the fsync/log-force operation across multiple concurrently committing transactions. Rather than issuing a separate synchronous disk flush for each transaction's commit record, the log manager buffers commit requests arriving within a short window and issues a single flush covering all their log records, then releases all waiting transactions simultaneously. This trades a small amount of added commit latency (waiting for the batch window) for dramatically higher throughput on I/O-latency-bound storage, since fsync cost is largely fixed per call regardless of the amount of data flushed.

### 1.6 Log Buffer Flushing and Force-at-Commit

The log manager accumulates records in an in-memory **log buffer** before writing to stable storage. Log records are flushed to disk when: (a) a transaction commits (force-at-commit), (b) the buffer fills, (c) a background log-writer thread flushes periodically, or (d) a page with a higher `pageLSN` than the current flushed LSN is about to be written to disk (enforcing the WAL invariant — this is the "log-flush-before-page-write" check in the buffer manager). The flushed LSN is a monotonically advancing watermark; the buffer manager must never write a data page whose `pageLSN` exceeds it.

### 1.7 Steal/No-Steal and Force/No-Force Policies

These two independent axes characterize buffer management policy relative to logging:

- **Steal vs. no-steal**: whether an uncommitted ("dirty") page can be written to disk before its transaction commits. **Steal** allows the buffer manager to evict dirty uncommitted pages under memory pressure, which requires **undo logging** capability (since the pre-commit write must be reversible on abort/crash). **No-steal** forbids this, simplifying recovery (no undo needed for that page) but constraining buffer replacement.
- **Force vs. no-force**: whether all pages modified by a transaction must be flushed to disk at commit time before acknowledging the commit. **Force** simplifies recovery (no redo needed) but adds synchronous I/O to every commit. **No-force** defers writes, requiring **redo logging** to reconstruct lost updates after a crash.

ARIES assumes the most general and highest-performance combination, **steal + no-force**, which requires both redo and undo logging — this is why ARIES needs the full three-pass recovery algorithm rather than a simpler scheme.

### 1.8 ARIES as Canonical Algorithm

ARIES (Algorithm for Recovery and Isolation Exploiting Semantics), developed by Mohan et al. at IBM, is the reference design underlying most production WAL implementations (e.g., conceptually mirrored in PostgreSQL's WAL, InnoDB's redo log, SQL Server's transaction log). Its three defining principles are: **write-ahead logging** (as above), **repeating history during redo** (redo every logged operation unconditionally during recovery, regardless of transaction outcome, to restore the exact pre-crash state before undoing losers), and **logging changes during undo** via compensation log records to ensure undo actions are themselves never repeated non-idempotently if a second crash occurs during recovery.

---

## 2. LSM Trees (Log-Structured Merge Trees)

### 2.1 Memtable

Writes are first applied to an in-memory, sorted structure called the **memtable**, commonly implemented as a **skip list** (LevelDB, RocksDB default), though some engines use balanced trees (red-black trees) or other ordered structures. The memtable serves reads and writes at memory speed and maintains sort order incrementally, avoiding the cost of sorting on every write. It has a configured size threshold (e.g., 64 MB), beyond which it is marked **immutable** and a new mutable memtable is created to absorb further writes.

### 2.2 Write-Ahead Log Alongside the Memtable

Because the memtable is volatile, every write is also appended to a **write-ahead log** (sometimes called the commit log) before or concurrently with the memtable insert, providing crash durability for data not yet flushed to an SSTable. On restart, the WAL is replayed to reconstruct the memtable's state. Once a memtable is flushed to a durable SSTable, its corresponding WAL segment can be garbage collected, since the data is now durable in SSTable form.

### 2.3 Immutable Memtable Flush to SSTables

When a memtable fills, it is frozen (immutable) and a background thread flushes it to disk as a **Sorted String Table (SSTable)** — an immutable, sorted, append-structured file. Because the memtable is already sorted, the flush is a simple sequential write with no sort step. SSTables are internally organized into data blocks plus a **block index** (often a sparse index mapping the first key of each block to the block's file offset), allowing binary search over the index followed by a single block read, rather than scanning the whole file. Some engines (e.g., RocksDB) add a top-level **index block** and optional **partitioned index** for very large SSTables.

### 2.4 Bloom Filters for Read-Path Pruning

Because a read (point lookup) may need to check many SSTables across levels, each SSTable typically carries a **Bloom filter** over its key set. A Bloom filter is a probabilistic set-membership structure with no false negatives and a tunable false-positive rate; checking it before doing an actual disk read on an SSTable allows the engine to skip SSTables that definitely do not contain the key, which is the dominant technique for controlling **read amplification** in LSM engines. Some systems (e.g., RocksDB) also support prefix Bloom filters for range scans with known prefixes.

### 2.5 Tombstones

Deletes in an LSM tree are not performed in place (the target key may live in an immutable SSTable on disk). Instead, a **tombstone** — a special marker record indicating "this key is deleted as of this sequence number" — is written, following the same write path as an ordinary put. Tombstones are resolved at read time (a tombstone shadows older versions of the key) and are only physically eliminated during **compaction**, when the tombstone and all older versions of the key it shadows can be dropped (subject to the tombstone's key not existing in any deeper, untouched level — otherwise the tombstone must be retained to avoid resurrecting stale data).

### 2.6 Compaction Strategies

Compaction merges SSTables to reclaim space from overwrites/deletes, bound the number of files a read must check, and maintain sort order across levels. Major strategies:

- **Leveled compaction**: SSTables are organized into levels (L0, L1, L2, …) with each level's total size an order of magnitude (commonly 10×) larger than the previous. Within a level (L1+), SSTables have non-overlapping key ranges. Compaction merges a file from level *N* with overlapping files in level *N+1*, producing new non-overlapping files. This minimizes space amplification and bounds read amplification (at most one file per level needs checking for L1+), at the cost of higher **write amplification** (each key may be rewritten once per level it passes through).
- **Size-tiered compaction**: SSTables of similar size are grouped into "tiers"; when enough similarly-sized tables accumulate at a tier, they are merged into a single larger table promoted to the next tier. This reduces write amplification relative to leveled compaction (fewer rewrites per key on average) but increases space amplification (more overlapping tables may need to be checked on read, and obsolete versions linger longer) and read amplification.
- **RocksDB's leveled-tiered hybrid** (and "universal compaction" as an explicit alternative mode): RocksDB's default leveled compaction actually tiers files within L0 (allowing some overlap/accumulation there, flushed directly from memtables) before transitioning to strict leveled organization from L1 onward — a pragmatic hybrid that amortizes memtable-flush bursts without paying full size-tiered space overhead deeper in the tree. RocksDB's "universal compaction" mode is a more explicit size-tiered strategy aimed at write-heavy, space-tolerant workloads.

### 2.7 Write and Read Amplification Trade-offs

**Write amplification** is the ratio of bytes actually written to physical storage versus bytes logically written by the application, driven by repeated rewriting of the same logical data across compaction passes. **Read amplification** is the number of physical storage reads (SSTable block reads) required to satisfy one logical read, driven by the number of levels/files that may contain the key. Leveled compaction favors low read/space amplification at the cost of higher write amplification; size-tiered compaction favors low write amplification at the cost of higher read/space amplification. This is the central tunable trade-off space of LSM tree design, and most production engines (RocksDB, Cassandra, ScyllaDB) expose the compaction strategy as a per-workload configuration choice.

---

## 3. B+Tree Maintenance

### 3.1 Node Splits and Merges

On insert, if a leaf (or internal node) would exceed its capacity, it undergoes a **split**: a new sibling node is allocated, roughly half the entries are moved to it, and a new separator key is **posted** (inserted) into the parent pointing to the new node — potentially cascading splits up to the root, where a split increases tree height by one. On delete, if a node's occupancy falls below a minimum threshold, it may be **merged** with a sibling (coalescing two underfull nodes into one, removing the separator from the parent) or undergo **redistribution** (rebalancing entries between the underfull node and a sibling without a full merge), depending on whether the sibling has enough slack. Deletion rebalancing is frequently made lazy or omitted entirely in production systems (allowing underfull nodes to persist) because merge operations are expensive relative to the benefit, and workloads with roughly balanced insert/delete rates self-correct through subsequent inserts.

### 3.2 Fill Factor and Node Occupancy

The **fill factor** is the target or minimum fraction of a node's capacity that should be occupied, commonly bounded between 50% (minimum, the classic B-tree invariant) and 100%. **Bulk loading** (see below) often targets a fill factor noticeably below 100% (e.g., 70–90%) deliberately, leaving slack for subsequent inserts to avoid immediate splits (this slack is sometimes explicitly called the **load factor** or fill-factor parameter in systems like PostgreSQL, SQL Server, and InnoDB). Low fill factor trades space efficiency for reduced split frequency and better insert locality.

### 3.3 Latch Coupling (Crabbing)

For concurrent tree traversal under a classic page-latching concurrency scheme, **latch coupling** (also called **crabbing**) acquires a latch on a child node *before* releasing the latch on its parent, ensuring no concurrent structural modification can invalidate the path being traversed. For read-only traversals, latches can typically be released immediately after acquiring the child's latch (no need to hold the parent). For modifying traversals (insert/delete), a conservative approach holds latches top-down until it is certain a given node will not split/merge (determined by checking whether the node has slack below/above the split/merge threshold); if a node is "safe" (won't need restructuring), ancestor latches can be released early — this optimistic release is often called the **safe node** optimization.

### 3.4 B-Link Trees (Right-Link Trees)

**B-link trees** augment each node with a **right-link pointer** to its right sibling at the same level, enabling a lock-free (or more precisely, latch-free for readers crossing a half-completed split) style of concurrent structure modification. During a split, the new right sibling can be made visible and linked before the parent's separator key is posted; a concurrent traverser who lands on the original node and doesn't find its target key can follow the right-link to reach the newly split-off sibling, rather than being blocked. This decouples the split of a node from the atomic update of its parent, allowing each step to be a separate, independently-latched or even lock-free operation (the technique underlying Lehman and Yao's classic concurrent B-tree algorithm), substantially improving concurrency over strict latch coupling.

### 3.5 Prefix/Suffix Truncation

**Separator keys** posted into parent nodes during a split do not need to be a full copy of the dividing key — they only need to be sufficient to correctly route searches, i.e., any value strictly between the maximum key of the left child and the minimum key of the right child. **Prefix truncation** (storing only the differing suffix relative to a common prefix) and **suffix truncation** (storing the shortest key that still separates the two subtrees, dropping trailing bytes not needed for discrimination) reduce the size of internal node entries, increasing fanout and reducing tree height. This is sometimes called **key compression** or (in the context of the minimal separator) **simple prefix B-trees**.

### 3.6 Bulk Loading

Rather than inserting rows one at a time (incurring a split cascade and poor locality), **bulk loading** builds a B+tree bottom-up from pre-sorted data: leaf pages are packed sequentially to the target fill factor, and internal levels are constructed directly from the resulting leaf boundaries without any split operations. This is dramatically faster than iterative insertion (avoiding repeated latching, splitting, and random I/O) and is the standard technique for initial index creation (`CREATE INDEX`) and bulk data loads in essentially all production RDBMSs.

### 3.7 Rebalancing Strategies

Beyond immediate merge-on-underflow, systems vary in rebalancing aggressiveness: **eager rebalancing** merges/redistributes immediately on underflow (strict occupancy guarantee, more write overhead); **lazy rebalancing** defers merges, tolerating underfull nodes until some background or opportunistic maintenance pass reclaims them (lower per-operation overhead, periodic housekeeping cost, used by many production systems including InnoDB and PostgreSQL to a degree). Some systems periodically run explicit **index rebuild/reorganize** operations as an offline or online maintenance task to restore compact occupancy and remove fragmentation accumulated from skewed insert/delete patterns.

### 3.8 Clustered vs. Non-Clustered Index Maintenance Costs

In a **clustered index**, the leaf level of the B+tree *is* the table's row storage, physically ordered by the index key; there is only one clustered index per table. Maintenance cost: every insert/update/delete directly manipulates the primary data storage, and a split moves actual row data, which is relatively expensive but means range scans on the clustering key are maximally sequential/efficient. In a **non-clustered (secondary) index**, leaf nodes store the index key plus a reference (row ID, or in clustered-primary-key systems like InnoDB, the primary key value) to the actual row stored elsewhere. Maintenance cost is lower per entry (leaf entries are small, fixed-size pointers/keys rather than full rows) but there can be many non-clustered indexes per table, each independently requiring split/merge maintenance on every write — and because the non-clustered index's logical order does not correspond to physical storage order of the referenced rows, point lookups via a non-clustered index incur an extra indirection (a second B+tree descent, or row lookup by RID) that clustered indexes avoid. Systems using a clustered primary key (InnoDB) also face **secondary index fan-out cost on primary key updates**, since every secondary index must be updated if the clustering key value changes.

---

## 4. Crash Recovery

### 4.1 ARIES Three-Phase Recovery

ARIES recovery proceeds in three sequential passes over the log after a crash:

1. **Analysis pass**: scans forward from the most recent checkpoint to reconstruct the **Transaction Table** (which transactions were active at crash time, and their last-LSN) and the **Dirty Page Table** (which pages were dirty, and the `recLSN` marking the earliest log record not yet reflected on disk for that page). This pass determines the **redo starting point** — the minimum `recLSN` across the final DPT — and which transactions are "losers" requiring undo.
2. **Redo pass**: starts from the redo starting point and replays every logged update whose effect is not already reflected in the corresponding page (checked by comparing the log record's LSN against the page's current `pageLSN`), **repeating history** unconditionally for all transactions, committed or not. This restores the exact physical database state as of the instant of the crash.
3. **Undo pass**: scans backward (following each loser transaction's last-LSN chain) undoing the actions of transactions that were active (uncommitted) at crash time, generating compensation log records as it goes.

### 4.2 Repeating History

The principle of **repeating history** means redo does not attempt to distinguish committed from uncommitted updates — it blindly reapplies every logged physical/physiological change (subject to the LSN-vs-pageLSN check for idempotence) to bring the database to its exact pre-crash state, including the (as yet undiscovered-as-losers) effects of transactions that will later be undone. This is what makes the subsequent undo pass correct: undo operates on a known, fully-reconstructed state rather than trying to reason about a partially-applied one.

### 4.3 Compensation Log Records (CLRs)

When undoing a loser transaction's update, ARIES writes a **Compensation Log Record** describing the undo action *before or as* it performs it. A CLR contains a field called the **UndoNextLSN** pointing to the LSN of the log record preceding the one just undone in that transaction's chain, skipping over it. CLRs are never themselves undone, which guarantees that **undo is idempotent**: if a second crash occurs during the undo pass, re-analysis and redo will replay the CLRs already written (redoing the undo actions, which is safe and correct), and the undo pass resumes using `UndoNextLSN` chains, so no action is undone twice and the total amount of work to complete recovery is strictly bounded regardless of how many times a crash recurs during recovery itself.

### 4.4 Dirty Page Table and Checkpoint-Based Bounding

The Dirty Page Table, captured and persisted at each fuzzy checkpoint, is the mechanism that bounds recovery work: because it records the minimum `recLSN` of any still-unflushed dirty page, the redo pass never needs to scan further back in the log than that point — all earlier updates are guaranteed already durable on disk. Without this bound, every recovery would need to scan the entire log from its beginning. The Transaction Table captured at checkpoint similarly bounds the backward scan needed to reconstruct per-transaction undo chains during analysis.

### 4.5 Redo-Undo Logging Rules

The **redo rule**: redo an update if the log record's LSN is greater than the affected page's current `pageLSN` (meaning the update is not yet reflected on disk) — otherwise skip it (already applied, avoiding duplicate/non-idempotent reapplication). The **undo rule**: for every update log record belonging to a loser transaction, generate the compensating action and a CLR, then continue backward using that transaction's LSN chain (or the CLR's UndoNextLSN if resuming after a prior partial undo) until reaching the transaction's begin record, at which point an **end record** is written and the transaction is fully removed from consideration.

### 4.6 Torn Write Protection (Double-Write Buffer)

Physical storage devices typically guarantee atomicity only at a sector/block granularity smaller than a full database page (e.g., a 512-byte or 4KB sector versus an 8KB or 16KB page); a crash mid-write can leave a page **torn** — part old version, part new version, internally inconsistent. InnoDB addresses this with the **doublewrite buffer**: before writing modified pages to their actual data-file locations, InnoDB first writes them sequentially to a contiguous doublewrite buffer area on disk (a safe, append-style write unlikely to itself be torn, or detectable if so), fsyncs that, and only then writes each page to its real location. If a crash tears a page during the real write, recovery detects the corruption (via checksum, see below) and restores the page from its intact doublewrite copy before beginning normal redo/undo. Other systems use alternative torn-write defenses, such as full-page logging (logging the entire before-image or after-image of a page, as PostgreSQL's `full_page_writes` does for the first modification after a checkpoint) to achieve the same end — ensuring a known-good page image is recoverable even if the in-place write was interrupted.

### 4.7 Checksums and Page Validation

Every persisted page typically carries a **checksum** (e.g., CRC32, Fletcher-based, or XOR-folded checksums depending on engine) computed over its contents and stored in the page header/footer. On every page read, the engine recomputes the checksum and compares it to the stored value; a mismatch signals **torn writes, bit rot, or other corruption** and triggers an error rather than silently operating on corrupt data. This is the detection complement to the doublewrite buffer's prevention/repair mechanism — checksums catch corruption that preventive measures didn't stop (e.g., storage-layer bit flips unrelated to torn writes), and are a prerequisite for recovery to trust that a page it is about to redo/undo against is the page it believes it is, rather than silently garbage.

# Technical Brief: Atomic Commitment, Logical Time, and Quorum Systems

## 5. Two-Phase Commit (2PC)

Two-phase commit is an atomic commitment protocol that ensures all participants in a distributed transaction either commit or abort uniformly, preserving the atomicity property of ACID across multiple resource managers.

### 5.1 Roles and basic protocol structure

One node acts as the **transaction coordinator** (or transaction manager); the remaining nodes are **participants** (resource managers, cohorts). The coordinator drives two phases:

**Phase 1 — Prepare/Vote phase.** The coordinator sends a `PREPARE` (or `VOTE-REQUEST`) message to all participants. Each participant checks whether it can locally guarantee the commit (constraint checks satisfied, locks held, no local failure), and if so, writes a **prepare record** to its write-ahead log and replies `VOTE-COMMIT`. If it cannot guarantee commit, it replies `VOTE-ABORT` and may unilaterally abort and release resources immediately, since no one has committed yet.

**Phase 2 — Commit/Abort phase.** If the coordinator receives `VOTE-COMMIT` from every participant, it writes its own **commit decision record** to its log and broadcasts `GLOBAL-COMMIT`. If any participant votes abort (or times out), the coordinator broadcasts `GLOBAL-ABORT`. Participants apply the decision, release locks, and send an `ACK`. The coordinator may discard transaction state once all acknowledgments are received.

### 5.2 Write-ahead logging and forced log writes

The defining durability mechanism is that each participant must **force the prepare record to stable storage (write-ahead log, WAL) before sending `VOTE-COMMIT`**. This is the standard write-ahead logging (WAL) rule applied to atomic commitment: a participant must never vote commit unless it can guarantee it will be able to commit even after a crash and restart, which requires the prepare record (including the redo/undo information needed to complete the transaction) to be durable first. Symmetrically, the coordinator must force its **commit record** to disk before sending `GLOBAL-COMMIT`, because once any participant acts on a commit decision, that decision must be recoverable even if the coordinator subsequently crashes.

### 5.3 The blocking problem

2PC's central defect is that it is a **blocking protocol** under coordinator failure. If a participant has voted commit (and is therefore in the **in-doubt** or "uncertain" state) and the coordinator crashes before sending the Phase 2 decision, that participant cannot unilaterally decide to commit or abort: committing without confirmation risks divergence from a possible coordinator abort decision, and aborting risks divergence from a possible commit decision already observed by other participants. The participant must hold all acquired locks and block indefinitely until the coordinator recovers or a human/administrative intervention occurs. This is formalized in the literature (Skeen, Gray) as 2PC's failure to be **non-blocking**: no protocol in the standard 2PC message pattern can guarantee progress under a coordinator crash combined with network partition, because a surviving participant cannot distinguish "coordinator committed and crashed before telling everyone" from "coordinator aborted and crashed before telling everyone" by communicating only with other participants.

### 5.4 In-doubt transactions and participant recovery

A transaction for which a participant has voted but not yet received the final decision is termed **in-doubt**. Recovery protocols address this via:

- **Coordinator recovery**: on restart, the coordinator reads its log; if a commit/abort decision record exists, it re-sends the decision (idempotently) to all participants (termination protocol). If only prepare messages were sent with no decision logged, it can safely abort (since it never committed).
- **Participant termination protocol**: a participant in-doubt after coordinator timeout may query other participants (**cooperative termination protocol**) to learn if any of them received a decision already; if even one participant knows the outcome, all can adopt it. If none know, they remain blocked.
- **Presumed-abort (PA)** optimization: the coordinator does not log or retain state for aborted transactions. If a participant queries about a transaction for which the coordinator has no record, it presumes abort. This allows the coordinator to skip writing abort records and skip sending ACKs for aborts, reducing log and message volume for the common case of symmetric read-dominated workloads where aborts are a terminal, "forgettable" state.
- **Presumed-commit (PC)** optimization: inverts the default — absence of coordinator state is interpreted as commit. This optimizes workloads where commits dominate, at the cost of requiring the coordinator to durably log the *participant list* before sending prepare (so it can answer queries about abort cases, which now require the asymmetric log record).

### 5.5 Three-phase commit (3PC) as a non-blocking extension

**Three-phase commit** (Skeen) inserts a **pre-commit** phase between vote collection and the final commit to eliminate blocking under certain failure assumptions. After collecting unanimous `VOTE-COMMIT`, the coordinator broadcasts a `PRE-COMMIT` message (rather than going straight to commit) and waits for acknowledgments before issuing the final `COMMIT`. This ensures that any participant that has reached the pre-commit state knows that *all* participants voted commit, so a newly elected coordinator (via a timeout-driven election among surviving participants) can inspect participant states and safely determine the correct outcome without waiting for the original coordinator: if any participant is in pre-commit or commit, the new coordinator can safely drive to commit; if none have gone beyond prepared, it can safely abort. 3PC achieves non-blocking termination under fail-stop failures in a synchronous network with bounded message delay, but does **not** solve the problem under network partitions — a partitioned minority can still make progress that contradicts the majority, violating consistency, so 3PC is rarely deployed in practice and is mostly of theoretical/pedagogical interest.

### 5.6 Relationship to distributed consensus

2PC is *not* a consensus protocol in the FLP/Paxos sense — it has no mechanism to make progress despite the failure of the coordinator, whereas consensus protocols like **Paxos** and **Raft** are designed explicitly to tolerate the failure of any minority of participants (including the leader/proposer) via **majority quorums** and **leader election**. 2PC assumes the coordinator's eventual recovery or manual intervention; it does not solve the general consensus problem.

Modern systems reconcile this by running **2PC over Paxos (or Raft) groups** rather than over single nodes, replacing "participant" with "a Paxos group replicating a shard." **Google Spanner** is the canonical example: each shard (tablet) is replicated via a **Paxos group** with a per-group leader, and multi-shard transactions use 2PC *across* Paxos groups, with the 2PC coordinator role held by one of the participating Paxos leaders. This hybridizes the two mechanisms: Paxos provides fault tolerance and non-blocking leader replacement *within* each shard (so a single node failure doesn't stall the shard), while 2PC provides atomicity *across* shards. The in-doubt/blocking problem of 2PC is thereby mitigated but not eliminated — it still blocks if an entire Paxos group (not just its leader) is unreachable, but single-node failures no longer cause global blocking since a new Paxos leader can be elected to resume the coordinator or participant role using state replicated via the Paxos log.

---

## 6. Logical Clocks

Logical clocks provide ordering of events in a distributed system without relying on synchronized physical clocks, addressing the fact that wall-clock time across independent nodes is subject to skew and drift.

### 6.1 Lamport clocks and happens-before

**Lamport timestamps** (Lamport, 1978) assign each event a scalar counter such that the counter respects the **happens-before relation** (→), a partial order defined by: (a) if events *a* and *b* occur on the same process and *a* precedes *b*, then *a → b*; (b) if *a* is the sending of a message and *b* is its receipt, *a → b*; (c) transitivity. The clock rule: each process increments its own counter for every local event, and when sending a message attaches its current counter value; on receipt, a process sets its counter to `max(local, received) + 1`. This guarantees the **clock consistency condition**: if *a → b* then `C(a) < C(b)`. The converse does not hold — `C(a) < C(b)` does not imply *a → b* — because Lamport clocks only produce a **total order consistent with causality**, collapsing concurrent (causally unrelated) events into an arbitrary order, typically broken by appending process IDs as a tiebreaker.

### 6.2 Vector clocks

**Vector clocks** (Fidge, Mattern) extend Lamport clocks to capture causality *exactly*, not just consistently. Each process *i* maintains a vector `V[1..N]` of counters, one per process. On a local event, process *i* increments `V[i]`. On sending, it attaches its full vector; on receipt, process *j* sets `V[j] = V[j] + 1` and then takes the elementwise maximum with the received vector for all other entries. Two events can be compared via the vector partial order: *a → b* **iff** `V(a) ≤ V(b)` elementwise with at least one strict inequality. If neither `V(a) ≤ V(b)` nor `V(b) ≤ V(a)` holds, the events are **concurrent**, denoted *a ∥ b* — this is the key capability vector clocks add over scalar Lamport clocks: the ability to *detect* concurrency (and hence potential write conflicts) rather than merely imposing an arbitrary total order over it. The cost is O(N) space per timestamp, which becomes problematic in systems with large or dynamic numbers of nodes.

### 6.3 Version vectors (Dynamo-style conflict detection)

**Version vectors** are the applied form of vector clocks used for **conflict detection in replicated, eventually-consistent data stores**, most notably Amazon **Dynamo** and its descendants (Riak, Voldemort, Cassandra's older designs). Rather than tracking every process's logical clock, a version vector attaches to each *object version* a map from replica/coordinator ID to a counter incremented each time that replica accepts a write to that object. When a replica receives two versions of an object, it compares their version vectors: if one dominates the other (elementwise ≥, strictly greater in at least one entry), the dominated version is causally stale and can be discarded (**causal subsumption**); if neither dominates, the versions are **concurrent (conflicting) siblings** that must be surfaced to the application (or merged via a CRDT-like reconciliation function) rather than silently overwritten. This is the basis of Dynamo's **"last write wins is insufficient" design philosophy** — version vectors let the system distinguish genuine concurrent updates needing application-level conflict resolution from simple causally-ordered updates needing no resolution. Dynamo additionally truncates version vectors (dropping the oldest clock entries) to bound their size, trading perfect conflict detection for bounded metadata overhead.

### 6.4 Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC)

**Hybrid Logical Clocks** (Kulkarni et al.) combine a physical wall-clock component with a logical counter to get the best of both: timestamps that are *causality-consistent* like Lamport clocks, but also *closely track physical time* so they can be used for human-meaningful event ordering, TTL expiration, and approximate real-time queries. An HLC timestamp is a pair `(pt, l)` where `pt` is drawn from the local physical clock and `l` is a logical component. The update rule on a local event or message receipt sets the new physical component to `max(local physical clock, pt of local HLC, pt of received HLC)`; if this maximum came from advancing the real clock (i.e., exceeds both prior HLC physical values), the logical counter resets to 0; otherwise, if ties occur at the same physical value, the logical counter increments, preserving the Lamport-style tie-break mechanism for events that are not separated by physical clock advancement. HLC timestamps are therefore **always within a small bounded offset of true physical time** (bounded by clock skew plus communication delay) while still satisfying the same consistency property as Lamport clocks (*a → b* ⟹ `HLC(a) < HLC(b)`). This mechanism underlies **CockroachDB**'s transaction timestamps (used alongside its uncertainty-interval-based concurrency control) and **MongoDB's** cluster-wide `ClusterTime`, both of which need timestamps that are both causally meaningful and roughly wall-clock-comparable without requiring tightly synchronized clocks.

### 6.5 Google TrueTime and bounded uncertainty intervals

**TrueTime**, used in **Google Spanner**, takes a fundamentally different approach: rather than purely logical counters, it exposes physical time directly but with an explicit, bounded **uncertainty interval**. The TrueTime API `TT.now()` does not return a single timestamp but an interval `[earliest, latest]` guaranteed to contain the true (unknown) absolute time at the moment of the call, with the interval width (epsilon, typically single-digit milliseconds) bounded by rigorous engineering: GPS and atomic clock (cesium) time references distributed across Google's infrastructure, continuous uncertainty-bound computation accounting for local oscillator drift since the last synchronization, and conservative error bounds. Spanner uses this for its **commit-wait** mechanism to achieve **external consistency** (a global ordering of transactions consistent with real-time precedence, stronger than ordinary linearizability extended to multi-key, multi-shard transactions): after choosing a commit timestamp `s` for a transaction, Spanner waits until `TT.now().earliest > s` is certain to have passed (i.e., waits out the uncertainty interval) before releasing the commit's effects/locks, guaranteeing that any transaction starting after this one observably commits sees a strictly later TrueTime-derived timestamp. This mechanism directly solves the problem that pure logical clocks cannot — giving timestamps that correspond to a *real*, boundedly-accurate global notion of time — at the cost of requiring specialized hardware infrastructure and accepting commit latency proportional to epsilon.

### 6.6 Reconciling causality and physical time

The three mechanisms above represent a spectrum: Lamport/vector clocks give exact logical causality with no relation to wall-clock time; TrueTime gives physical time with bounded, hardware-enforced uncertainty but no inherent causality tracking (causality is instead enforced operationally via commit-wait); HLC sits in between, deriving a single scalar-like timestamp that is simultaneously a valid logical clock (causality-respecting) and an approximation of physical time usable for cross-system comparisons, without requiring atomic clocks or GPS receivers. Systems choose among these based on whether they need hardware-free deployability (HLC, vector clocks) versus the strongest real-time external consistency guarantees achievable only with bounded-uncertainty physical time sources (TrueTime).

---

## 7. Quorum Systems

Quorum systems provide availability and consistency trade-offs in replicated systems by requiring operations to be acknowledged by a subset ("quorum") of replicas rather than all of them.

### 7.1 Quorum intersection and the R + W > N rule

A **quorum system** over a set of N replicas defines, for each operation type, a minimum number of replicas that must participate. For read/write replicated systems (as formalized in Gifford's quorum consensus and used in Dynamo-style systems), let **N** be the replication factor, **W** the write quorum size, and **R** the read quorum size. The fundamental correctness condition is the **quorum intersection property**: any two quorums (e.g., a write quorum and a subsequent read quorum) must share at least one common replica, guaranteeing that a read quorum always overlaps with the most recent committed write quorum and therefore can observe the latest write (combined with per-replica versioning to identify which observed value is newest). This is formalized as **R + W > N**: if this inequality holds, any read quorum and any write quorum must intersect by the pigeonhole principle, since two disjoint sets of sizes R and W within a universe of size N would require R + W ≤ N. Systems also typically require **W > N/2** to ensure write quorums intersect each other, preventing two concurrent writes from both succeeding without being aware of each other (preventing "split-brain" writes to disjoint replica subsets).

### 7.2 Strict quorums vs. sloppy quorums

A **strict quorum** requires the quorum to be composed specifically of the designated, fixed set of N replicas that own a given key/partition — if fewer than the required quorum size of that fixed set are reachable, the operation fails, preserving strong consistency guarantees but sacrificing availability during partition or node failure.

Amazon **Dynamo** introduced the **sloppy quorum** as an availability-favoring relaxation: instead of requiring responses specifically from the N nodes that are the "natural" owners of a key (per the consistent hashing ring), a sloppy quorum accepts responses from the first W (or R) *healthy* nodes encountered while walking the ring, regardless of whether they are among the key's designated owners. This trades strict consistency (and the clean quorum-intersection guarantee above, which assumes a fixed replica set) for **always-writable availability** — writes succeed even when some or all of a key's designated replicas are down, by temporarily storing data on substitute nodes.

### 7.3 Hinted handoff

**Hinted handoff** is the complementary repair mechanism for sloppy quorums: when a write lands on a substitute node because a designated owner was unreachable, the substitute stores the data along with a "hint" indicating the true intended owner. Once the designated owner recovers and becomes reachable again, the substitute node detects this (e.g., via periodic gossip or anti-entropy checks) and transfers ("hands off") the hinted data to the rightful owner, then deletes its local copy. This restores the system to its designated replica placement over time without blocking writes during the owner's downtime.

### 7.4 Read repair

**Read-repair** is an anti-entropy mechanism triggered at read time: when a read quorum is collected, if the R responding replicas return divergent versions (detectable via version vectors, vector clocks, or simple timestamps), the coordinator determines the correct/latest version (through version-vector dominance or application-level reconciliation) and proactively writes that version back to the stale replicas before or after returning the result to the client. This incrementally converges replicas toward consistency driven by read traffic patterns, complementing periodic background anti-entropy processes (e.g., Merkle-tree-based reconciliation) that handle keys that are rarely read.

### 7.5 Majority quorums in consensus protocols

**Paxos** and **Raft** use a specific, stricter instantiation of the quorum concept: the **majority quorum**, requiring any quorum to contain more than half of the N replicas (⌊N/2⌋ + 1). The critical property this guarantees is that **any two majority quorums must intersect in at least one node**, which is what allows these protocols to guarantee **safety** (agreement) across leader changes: a newly elected leader, by contacting a majority during its election phase (Raft's `RequestVote` / Paxos's Phase 1 `Prepare`), is guaranteed to overlap with any previous majority that committed a value, and can therefore discover the highest-numbered previously accepted or committed proposal and preserve it rather than allowing it to be lost or overwritten. This differs from Dynamo-style quorums in that majority quorums are used to achieve strict linearizable consensus on a single sequence of values/commands (the replicated log), rather than merely to bound staleness in a key-value read/write path; the quorum size is fixed at a strict majority rather than being independently tunable as separate R and W parameters.

### 7.6 Witness replicas / non-voting members

**Witness replicas** (sometimes called non-voting members, or in some systems "arbiters"/"quorum-only nodes") participate in the voting/quorum-counting process for availability and fault-tolerance purposes — i.e., they can cast votes in leader elections or acknowledge writes to help reach quorum size — without storing the full replicated state (data) themselves, or in some variants, storing state but never becoming eligible to serve as leader. The purpose is to allow a deployment to achieve odd-numbered quorum sizes (avoiding split-vote ties) and meet fault-tolerance targets (e.g., tolerating one full data-replica failure) more cheaply, since witnesses need only track metadata (e.g., the latest log position/term they've acknowledged) rather than full data, reducing storage and sometimes compute/network cost relative to a full voting data replica. This pattern appears in Raft-based systems (e.g., non-voting learner members, or dedicated witness/arbiter nodes in MongoDB replica sets) and in some Paxos deployments as a cost-efficient way to break ties and maintain quorum availability without tripling full data storage.

### 7.7 Flexible quorums and Paxos Quorum Leases

**Flexible quorums** (Howard, Malkhi, Spiegelman) observe that classic Paxos/Raft conflate two distinct quorum roles that do not need to use the same quorum size: the **phase-1 quorum** (used during leader election / `Prepare` to discover prior accepted values) and the **phase-2 quorum** (used during normal-case command replication / `Accept`). The flexible-quorum result shows that correctness only requires phase-1 and phase-2 quorums to intersect (not that either individually be a strict majority), enabling configurations like **"grid quorums"** or asymmetric splits — e.g., a small phase-2 quorum for fast, low-latency normal-case writes, paired with a larger phase-1 quorum used only during the rarer leader-election path, as long as every phase-1 quorum intersects every phase-2 quorum. This can reduce the latency or replica count needed for the common-case write path at the cost of a more expensive (larger-quorum) leader-election path.

**Paxos Quorum Leases** (PQL) extend this idea to optimize **local, quorum-free reads**: a designated subset of replicas (the "lease holders," themselves forming a quorum-sized or other designated set) is granted a lease guaranteeing that no write will be accepted without their participation for the lease's duration. Any replica holding a valid lease can then serve **linearizable reads locally**, without contacting any other replica or performing a read-quorum round-trip, because the lease guarantees no conflicting write could have completed without that replica's knowledge. This trades a small amount of write-path overhead (writes must now also contact lease-holders) for substantially reduced read latency, which is advantageous in read-heavy workloads — directly analogous to how read quorums are normally required for linearizability in quorum-replicated systems, but amortizes that cost via a time-bounded lease rather than paying it on every read.
